claim: Glioblastoma is a highly aggressive brain tumor.
source: Glioblastoma is a highly aggressive brain tumor.
evidence: This is a well-established characterization of glioblastoma in the medical literature.

claim: Current standard-of-care for glioblastoma results in a marginal therapeutic outcome, partly due to acquirement of resistance and insufficient blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration of chemotherapeutics.
source: Current standard-of-care results in a marginal therapeutic outcome, partly due to acquirement of resistance and insufficient blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration of chemotherapeutics.
evidence: This statement reflects established clinical knowledge about glioblastoma treatment challenges.

claim: dPGS is able to cross the BBB, bind to P/L-selectins and accumulate selectively in intracranial tumors.
source: dPGS is able to cross the BBB, bind to P/L-selectins and accumulate selectively in intracranial tumors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing dPGS accumulation in intracranial tumors.

claim: P-selectin is expressed on tumor endothelium.
source: We show that dPGS has dual targeting properties, as we found that P-selectin is not only expressed on tumor endothelium but also on glioblastoma cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in the manuscript.

claim: P-selectin is expressed on glioblastoma cells.
source: We show that dPGS has dual targeting properties, as we found that P-selectin is not only expressed on tumor endothelium but also on glioblastoma cells.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry and immunohistochemistry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Combination of dPGS-PTX with TSP-1 PM resulted in a remarkable synergistic anticancer effect on intracranial human and murine glioblastoma.
source: This combination resulted in a remarkable synergistic anticancer effect on intracranial human and murine glioblastoma via induction of Fas and Fas-L, with no side effects compared to free PTX or temozolomide.
evidence: This is supported by survival data and tumor growth measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: The combination therapy induces Fas and Fas-L expression.
source: This combination resulted in a remarkable synergistic anticancer effect on intracranial human and murine glioblastoma via induction of Fas and Fas-L, with no side effects compared to free PTX or temozolomide.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing increased Fas and Fas-L expression.

claim: The combination therapy has no side effects compared to free PTX or temozolomide.
source: This combination resulted in a remarkable synergistic anticancer effect on intracranial human and murine glioblastoma via induction of Fas and Fas-L, with no side effects compared to free PTX or temozolomide.
evidence: This is supported by body weight measurements, blood tests, and motor coordination tests presented in the manuscript.

claim: Glioblastoma is the most common form of primary brain tumor.
source: Glioblastoma is the most common form of primary brain tumor and is one of the most aggressive forms of cancer (Wen and Kesari, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wen and Kesari, 2008.

claim: Glioblastoma is one of the most aggressive forms of cancer.
source: Glioblastoma is the most common form of primary brain tumor and is one of the most aggressive forms of cancer (Wen and Kesari, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wen and Kesari, 2008.

claim: Without treatment, the median survival for glioblastoma is approximately 3 months.
source: Without treatment, the median survival is approximately 3 months (Schapira, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schapira, 2007.

claim: The current standard of treatment for glioblastoma involves maximal surgical resection followed by concurrent radiation therapy and chemotherapy with temozolomide.
source: The current standard of treatment involves maximal surgical resection followed by concurrent radiation therapy and chemotherapy with the DNA alkylating agent temozolomide (TMZ) (Stupp et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stupp et al., 2005.

claim: With the current standard treatment regimen, the median survival for glioblastoma is increased to approximately 14 months.
source: With this regimen, the median survival is increased to approximately 14 months (Stupp et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stupp et al., 2005.

claim: Glioblastoma's diffusive and invasive nature makes complete removal of the tumor by conventional surgery nearly impossible.
source: Glioblastoma's diffusive and invasive nature makes complete removal of the tumor by conventional surgery nearly impossible.
evidence: This is established knowledge about glioblastoma characteristics.

claim: Tumor recurrence is inevitable for glioblastoma.
source: Therefore, tumor recurrence is inevitable and only 1.8% of patients survive more than three years (Scott et al., 1998; Wen and Kesari, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Scott et al., 1998 and Wen and Kesari, 2008.

claim: Only 1.8% of glioblastoma patients survive more than three years.
source: Therefore, tumor recurrence is inevitable and only 1.8% of patients survive more than three years (Scott et al., 1998; Wen and Kesari, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Scott et al., 1998 and Wen and Kesari, 2008.

claim: Various treatments using cytotoxic chemotherapy have shown disappointing results with an average overall survival of 3–9 months for recurrent glioblastoma.
source: Various other treatments using cytotoxic chemotherapy have shown disappointing results with an average overall survival (OS) of 3–9 months (Lamborn et al., 2008; Yung et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lamborn et al., 2008 and Yung et al., 2000.

claim: Bevacizumab was FDA-approved for the treatment of recurrent glioblastoma in 2009.
source: Additionally, bevacizumab, an anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) monoclonal antibody, was FDA-approved for the treatment of recurrent glioblastoma in 2009 (Kreisl et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kreisl et al., 2009.

claim: Treatment with bevacizumab among patients with newly diagnosed glioblastoma did not exhibit improvement in overall survival.
source: Although progression-free survival was slightly prolonged and an overall lowering of glucocorticoid requirements to control tumor-related edema was shown in patients with recurrent glioblastoma (Friedman et al., 2009), treatment with bevacizumab among patients with newly diagnosed glioblastoma did not exhibit improvement in OS of patients (Chinot et al., 2014; Gilbert et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chinot et al., 2014 and Gilbert et al., 2014.

claim: 30–60% of glioblastoma patients develop resistance to conventional therapy.
source: The high prevalence of resistance to conventional therapy in glioblastoma (30–60% of patients)(Weller et al., 2010) and poor outcome have led to several studies screening for new potential drugs that typically target other vital cellular functions.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Weller et al., 2010.

claim: Mitotic inhibitors, such as paclitaxel, were found to be among the most potent drugs for glioblastoma.
source: Mitotic inhibitors, such as paclitaxel (PTX), were found to be among the most potent drugs (Jiang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jiang et al., 2014.

claim: PTX binds to polymerized tubulin and inhibits the dissociation rate, leading to M phase cell cycle arrest.
source: This class of drug binds to polymerized tubulin and inhibits the dissociation rate, leading to M phase cell cycle arrest (Schiff et al., 1979).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schiff et al., 1979.

claim: PTX was shown to be highly potent against glioblastoma cells in vitro.
source: PTX was shown to be highly potent against glioblastoma cells in vitro (Cahan et al., 1994), but systemic delivery was associated with poor pharmacokinetics and neurotoxicity (Berger et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cahan et al., 1994.

claim: Systemic delivery of PTX was associated with poor pharmacokinetics and neurotoxicity.
source: PTX was shown to be highly potent against glioblastoma cells in vitro (Cahan et al., 1994), but systemic delivery was associated with poor pharmacokinetics and neurotoxicity (Berger et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Berger et al., 1997.

claim: Hypersensitivity to PTX was attributed to its polyoxyethylated castor oil solubilizing vehicle, Cremophor EL.
source: Furthermore, hypersensitivity was an additional toxicity which was not attributed to the drug itself, but rather to its polyoxyethylated castor oil solubilizing vehicle, Cremophor EL (CrEL) (Mielke et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mielke et al., 2005.

claim: Clinically significant neurotoxicity from PTX appears after administration of a cumulative dose of around 1,500 mg/m2.
source: Clinically significant neurotoxicity appears after administration of a cumulative dose of around 1,500 mg/m2 (Briasoulis et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Briasoulis et al., 2002.

claim: A well-designed polymeric drug delivery system improves the therapeutic index of anticancer agents.
source: A well-designed polymeric drug delivery system (DDS) improves the therapeutic index of anticancer agents.
evidence: This is established knowledge in drug delivery research.

claim: An ideal DDS can increase the half-life of low-molecular-weight drugs, improve water-solubility and cause selective tumor tissue accumulation.
source: An ideal DDS can increase the half-life of low-molecular-weight drugs, improve water-solubility (i.e., CrEL-free formulations) and cause selective tumor tissue accumulation, all while enhancing anticancer efficacy, reducing toxicity and limiting drug resistance (Markovsky et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Markovsky et al., 2012.

claim: Drug delivery systems exploit the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect.
source: These delivery systems exploit the natural (blood circulation and extravasation-dependent targeting – 'passive') distribution pattern of a drug-carrier in vivo, which is based upon the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect (Matsumura and Maeda, 1986).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Matsumura and Maeda, 1986.

claim: Blood circulation and extravasation-dependent targeting of DDS to brain tumors does not lead to sufficient drug penetration to the tumor.
source: Previous studies have shown that blood circulation and extravasation-dependent targeting of DDS to brain tumors does not lead to sufficient drug penetration to the tumor, and thus results in very little improvement in therapeutic efficacy (Muldoon et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Muldoon et al., 2007.

claim: dPGS nanocarriers bind and inhibit both L-selectin and P-selectin.
source: We have previously shown that dPGS nanocarriers, depending on size and degree of sulfation of the polymer core, bind and inhibit both L-selectin and P-selectin (Dernedde et al., 2010; Khandare et al., 2010; Sousa-Herves et al., 2015; Weinhart et al., 2011a, Weinhart et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Selectins are carbohydrate-binding proteins that are physiologically expressed on the surface of endothelial cells, activated platelets and leukocytes.
source: Selectins are carbohydrate-binding proteins that are physiologically expressed on the surface of endothelial cells (P-selectin and E-selectin), activated platelets (P-selectin) and leukocytes (L-selectin) (Läubli and Borsig, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Läubli and Borsig, 2010.

claim: Selectins are involved in tumor cell binding and promote their invasion by supporting a permissive metastatic microenvironment.
source: Selectins are also involved in tumor cell binding and promote their invasion by supporting a permissive metastatic microenvironment and protecting them from recognition by immune cells (Preusser et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Preusser et al., 2012.

claim: The dPGS used in this study consists of 90% sulfate groups and a 5 KDa molecular weight core.
source: To target glioblastoma, we have chosen dPGS with the highest affinity to selectins, which consists of 90% sulfate groups and a 5 KDa molecular weight core (Dernedde et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dernedde et al., 2010.

claim: Expression of P-selectin by glioblastoma cells was not previously reported.
source: To the best of our knowledge, expression of P-selectin by glioblastoma cells was not previously reported.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the finding based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: dPG forms three-dimensional hyperbranched nanostructures that have been shown to efficiently extravasate through the compromised BBB.
source: Utilizing a dendritic polyglycerol (dPG)-based structure as the DDS allows us to take advantage of its unique architecture. dPG forms three-dimensional hyperbranched nanostructures that have been shown before to efficiently extravasate through the compromised BBB (Ofek et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ofek et al., 2016.

claim: dPG nanostructures are water-soluble, easily tuned in size and functional groups, and synthesized on a kilogram scale.
source: They are also water-soluble, easily tuned in size and functional groups, and synthesized on a kilogram scale (Calderón et al., 2014; Calderón et al., 2011; Hussain et al., 2013; Weinhart et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: TSP-1 is a key endogenous angiogenesis inhibitor.
source: Thrombospondin-1 (TSP-1) is a key endogenous angiogenesis inhibitor, and its expression is often lost or decreased throughout malignant transformation (Sargiannidou et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sargiannidou et al., 2001.

claim: TSP-1 expression is often lost or decreased throughout malignant transformation.
source: Thrombospondin-1 (TSP-1) is a key endogenous angiogenesis inhibitor, and its expression is often lost or decreased throughout malignant transformation (Sargiannidou et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sargiannidou et al., 2001.

claim: In gliomas, TSP-1 downregulation results in accelerated disease.
source: In gliomas, TSP-1 downregulation results in accelerated disease (Hsu et al., 1996) and loss of TSP-1 correlates with transition from low-grade astrocytoma to glioblastoma (Almog et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hsu et al., 1996.

claim: Loss of TSP-1 correlates with transition from low-grade astrocytoma to glioblastoma.
source: In gliomas, TSP-1 downregulation results in accelerated disease (Hsu et al., 1996) and loss of TSP-1 correlates with transition from low-grade astrocytoma to glioblastoma (Almog et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Almog et al., 2009.

claim: The anti-angiogenic activity of TSP-1 is predominantly attributed to type one thrombospondin repeats (TSRs) that interact with CD36.
source: The anti-angiogenic activity of TSP-1 is predominantly attributed to type one thrombospondin repeats (TSRs) that interact with a fatty acid translocase receptor on the endothelial cell membrane, CD36 (Simantov and Silverstein, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Simantov and Silverstein, 2003.

claim: TSRs mimetic peptides have been successfully used to block angiogenesis and tumor growth in preclinical models.
source: TSRs mimetic peptides have been successfully used to block angiogenesis and tumor growth in preclinical models (Campbell et al., 2011; Rusk et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Campbell et al., 2011 and Rusk et al., 2006.

claim: ABT-510 is a nonapeptide with a single D-isoleucine replacement that resulted in a 1,000-fold increase of its anti-angiogenic activity.
source: ABT-510 (Abbott Laboratories) is a nonapeptide with a single D-isoleucine replacement that resulted in a 1,000-fold increase of its anti-angiogenic activity (Haviv et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Haviv et al., 2005.

claim: ABT-510-dependent apoptosis of tumor endothelial cells was shown to be induced by their upregulation of Fas ligand.
source: ABT-510-dependent apoptosis of tumor endothelial cells was shown to be induced by their upregulation of Fas ligand, and was amplified by low doses of chemotherapeutic agents since the latter increased endothelial cells presentation of CD95 death receptor, an effect seen with docetaxel (DTX) above 1 nM (Yap et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yap et al., 2005.

claim: ABT-510 was shown to normalize tumor vasculature and enhance the delivery and efficacy of both cisplatin and PTX in a syngeneic model of ovarian cancer.
source: The peptide was also shown to normalize tumor vasculature, and thereby enhance the delivery and efficacy of both cisplatin and PTX in a syngeneic model of ovarian cancer (Campbell et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Campbell et al., 2010.

claim: ABT-510 mitigated orthotopic glioma growth in a mouse model by increasing apoptosis in tumor microvascular endothelial cells.
source: ABT-510 mitigated orthotopic glioma growth in a mouse model by increasing apoptosis in tumor microvascular endothelial cells (Campbell et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Campbell et al., 2010.

claim: In a phase I clinical trial for glioblastoma, ABT-510 exhibited a favorable safety profile at a dose of up to 200 mg daily.
source: In a phase I clinical trial for the treatment of newly-diagnosed glioblastoma in combination with the standard of care (i.e., TMZ and radiation), ABT-510 exhibited a favorable safety profile at a dose of up to 200 mg daily for 6 days and additional 4 weeks as monotherapy (Nabors et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nabors et al., 2010.

claim: A phase I clinical trial showed ABT-510 has a poor pharmacokinetic profile with only a one hour clearance half-life.
source: However, another phase I clinical trial showed a poor pharmacokinetic profile of the peptide, demonstrating only a one hour clearance half-life (Hoekstra et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hoekstra et al., 2005.

claim: ABT-898 is a second-generation octapeptide with improved potency and slower clearance compared to ABT-510.
source: A second-generation octapeptide was developed (ABT-898) with improved potency and slower clearance (Henkin and Volpert, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Henkin and Volpert, 2011.

claim: ABT-898 has been evaluated in preclinical models of epithelial ovarian cancer and uveal melanoma in mice.
source: Thus far, ABT-898 has been evaluated in preclinical models of epithelial ovarian cancer and of uveal melanoma in mice (Campbell et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2012) and in treatment of spontaneously-occurring soft tissue sarcoma in dogs (Sahora et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Campbell et al., 2011 and Wang et al., 2012.

claim: ABT-898 was efficacious in preclinical models of ovarian cancer, uveal melanoma, and soft tissue sarcoma.
source: Thus far, ABT-898 has been evaluated in preclinical models of epithelial ovarian cancer and of uveal melanoma in mice (Campbell et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2012) and in treatment of spontaneously-occurring soft tissue sarcoma in dogs (Sahora et al., 2012). It was efficacious in all these settings.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Campbell et al., 2011, Wang et al., 2012, and Sahora et al., 2012.

claim: TSP-1 PM was delivered at a high dose of 100 mg/kg in this study.
source: TSP-1 PM was delivered at a high dose of 100 mg/kg.
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript and confirmed by the methods section.

claim: PTX was delivered at a reduced accumulated dose of 90 mg/kg in this study.
source: PTX was delivered at a reduced accumulated dose of 90 mg/kg.
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript and confirmed by the methods section.

claim: The PTX dose used in this study (90 mg/kg) correlates to 270 mg/m2, which is considerably lower than the maximal tolerated cumulative dose reported.
source: This correlates to 270 mg/m2, which is considerably lower than the maximal tolerated cumulative dose reported (Briasoulis et al., 2002).
evidence: This is based on a calculation and comparison to data from Briasoulis et al., 2002.

claim: The combination therapy was well tolerated by treated mice, with no neurological or systemic toxicities demonstrated.
source: This combination therapy was well tolerated by treated mice, with no neurological or systemic toxicities demonstrated.
evidence: This is supported by body weight, blood test, and motor coordination data presented in the manuscript.

claim: dPGS-PTX and dPG-PTX had approximately 1 mol of PTX per mol of conjugate.
source: The resulting sulfated targeted conjugate dPGS-PTX and control dPG-PTX had approximately 1 mol of PTX per mol of conjugate, as estimated by 1H NMR (Table 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: dPGS-PTX had a hydrodynamic diameter of about 46 nm.
source: dPGS-PTX had a hydrodynamic diameter of about 46 nm which is ideal for exploiting the EPR effect.
evidence: This is supported by DLS measurements shown in Figure 1C and Table 1.

claim: dPG-PTX had a hydrodynamic diameter of about 4 nm.
source: dPG-PTX was smaller, with a hydrodynamic diameter of about 4 nm.
evidence: This is supported by DLS measurements shown in Figure 1C and Table 1.

claim: The size of dPGS-PTX was validated by SEM to be 50 nm.
source: The size of dPGS-PTX was further validated by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (Figure 1D). Similarly to the size obtained by the DLS, dPGS-PTX was shown to have a diameter of 50 nm.
evidence: This is supported by SEM imaging shown in Figure 1D.

claim: dPGS-PTX had a zeta potential of about −47 mV.
source: As expected, zeta potential measurements for dPGS-PTX, containing 90% surface sulfate groups and 5% amine groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), showed a substantial negative charge of about −47 mV, while dPG-PTX, containing 10% amine surface groups and 90% of the mostly non-ionized hydroxyl groups, had a zeta potential of + 16.5 mV, similar to previous reports of dPG bearing the same percentage of cationic groups (Khandare et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by zeta potential measurements shown in Table 1.

claim: dPG-PTX had a zeta potential of +16.5 mV.
source: As expected, zeta potential measurements for dPGS-PTX, containing 90% surface sulfate groups and 5% amine groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), showed a substantial negative charge of about −47 mV, while dPG-PTX, containing 10% amine surface groups and 90% of the mostly non-ionized hydroxyl groups, had a zeta potential of + 16.5 mV, similar to previous reports of dPG bearing the same percentage of cationic groups (Khandare et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by zeta potential measurements shown in Table 1.

claim: A continuous PTX release was observed from dPGS-PTX at pH 2 and pH 5.
source: As expected, a continuous PTX release was observed at pH two and pH 5, while marginal PTX release was detected at pH seven or in plasma after 24 hr (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Marginal PTX release was detected from dPGS-PTX at pH 7 or in plasma after 24 hr.
source: As expected, a continuous PTX release was observed at pH two and pH 5, while marginal PTX release was detected at pH seven or in plasma after 24 hr (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: dPGS-PTX rapidly internalized into glioblastoma cells within minutes.
source: Flow cytometry analysis evaluating the uptake of IDCC-labeled dendritic conjugates demonstrated that they exhibit different internalization kinetics. dPGS-PTX-IDCC rapidly internalized into the cells within minutes, whereas the non-targeted conjugate, dPG-PTX-IDCC, internalized after more than 4 hr (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: dPG-PTX internalized into glioblastoma cells after more than 4 hr.
source: Flow cytometry analysis evaluating the uptake of IDCC-labeled dendritic conjugates demonstrated that they exhibit different internalization kinetics. dPGS-PTX-IDCC rapidly internalized into the cells within minutes, whereas the non-targeted conjugate, dPG-PTX-IDCC, internalized after more than 4 hr (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Treatment with P-selectin inhibitor prior to treatment with dendritic conjugates inhibited dPGS-PTX-IDCC uptake in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Treatment with the P-selectin inhibitor prior to treatment with the dendritic conjugates inhibited dPGS-PTX-IDCC uptake in a dose-dependent manner, while not affecting the uptake of dPG-PTX-IDCC (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: P-selectin inhibitor did not affect the uptake of dPG-PTX-IDCC.
source: Treatment with the P-selectin inhibitor prior to treatment with the dendritic conjugates inhibited dPGS-PTX-IDCC uptake in a dose-dependent manner, while not affecting the uptake of dPG-PTX-IDCC (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: dPGS-PTX internalizes into cells via P-selectin.
source: This demonstrated that dPGS-PTX internalizes into the cells via P-selectin.
evidence: This is inferred from the P-selectin inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: dPGS-PTX internalized into tumor spheroids more rapidly and efficiently compared to dPG-PTX.
source: Similar to the results received in 2D culture, dPGS-PTX internalized into the spheroids more rapidly and efficiently compared to dPG-PTX (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data of tumor spheroids shown in Figure 2C.

claim: U-87 MG cells expressed high P-Selectin levels on their surface.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, U-87 MG expressed high P-Selectin levels on their surface.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: P-Selectin overexpression was observed in all tested human and murine glioblastoma cell lines.
source: Surprisingly, P-Selectin overexpression was observed in all tested human and murine samples (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: P-Selectin was highly expressed in human U-87 MG and murine GL261 tumors.
source: P-Selectin was highly expressed in human U-87 MG and murine GL261 tumors, whereas almost no positive staining was observed in the adjacent normal brain (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Almost no P-selectin positive staining was observed in the adjacent normal brain.
source: P-Selectin was highly expressed in human U-87 MG and murine GL261 tumors, whereas almost no positive staining was observed in the adjacent normal brain (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: P-selectin was abundantly expressed in glioblastoma patient specimens.
source: P-selectin was also found to be abundantly expressed in glioblastoma patient specimens (Figure 3B), suggesting a clinical relevance of our therapeutic approach.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: P-selectin expression levels are lowest in the brain among healthy tissues.
source: Indeed, when looking at SELP expression in different healthy tissues in the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) collection, we found that its levels are lowest in the brain (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on analysis of GTEx data.

claim: P-selectin expression levels are markedly increased in gliomas compared to healthy brain tissue.
source: The expression levels of P-selectin were found to be markedly increased in gliomas compared to healthy brain tissue and further increased in glioblastomas. The resulting medians are 3.3234e-05, 1.8100e-04 and 9.4268e-04 for healthy tissue, lower grade glioma and glioblastoma, respectively (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by TCGA and GTEx data analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: P-selectin expression is further increased in glioblastomas compared to lower grade gliomas.
source: The expression levels of P-selectin were found to be markedly increased in gliomas compared to healthy brain tissue and further increased in glioblastomas. The resulting medians are 3.3234e-05, 1.8100e-04 and 9.4268e-04 for healthy tissue, lower grade glioma and glioblastoma, respectively (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by TCGA and GTEx data analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: P-selectin expression correlated with survival of glioblastoma patients.
source: A gene-expression-based survival analysis using TCGA data obtained from cBioPortal showed that P-selectin expression correlated with survival of glioblastoma patients (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Both dPGS-PTX and dPG-PTX induce cell cycle arrest at the G2/M phase.
source: A time-dependent increase in G2/M population was observed in all treatment groups, indicating that the conjugates induce cell cycle arrest at the G2/M phase (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: PTX retains its anti-mitotic activity in both dPGS-PTX and dPG-PTX conjugates.
source: These results suggest that PTX retains its anti-mitotic activity both in dPGS-PTX and dPG-PTX conjugates.
evidence: This is inferred from the cell cycle arrest data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: dPGS-PTX induces formation of microtubule bundles in cells.
source: Confocal images of cells following 8 hr incubation in the presence of dPGS-PTX show formation of microtubule bundles right before mitosis in a large population of the cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Both dendritic conjugates induced cell death at a similar extent as the free drug in U-87 MG, U251, and HUVEC cells after 72 hours.
source: Seventy-two hours following incubation, both dendritic conjugates induced cell death at a similar extent as the free drug in all cell types tested; U-87 MG and U251 glioblastoma cells and primary human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVEC) (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figures 4C-E.

claim: One hour following systemic administration, dPGS-PTX-IDCC evidently accumulated at the intracranial tumor.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, one hour following systemic administration, dPGS-PTX-IDCC evidently accumulated at the mCherry-labeled tumor.
evidence: This is supported by intravital fluorescence imaging shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Twenty-four hours after administration, substantial amount of dPGS-PTX-IDCC was still located at the intracranial tumor.
source: Twenty-four hours later, substantial amount of the conjugate was still located at the intracranial tumor, as exhibited by a strong fluorescence signal (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by intravital fluorescence imaging shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Preferable accumulation at the tumor site was not observed following systemic delivery of dPG-PTX.
source: Preferable accumulation at the tumor site was not observed following systemic delivery of dPG-PTX, which relies upon passive extravasation-dependent targeting alone (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by intravital fluorescence imaging shown in Figure 5A.

claim: One hour following injection, dPGS-PTX-IDCC was clearly visualized within the tumor tissue but not in the normal brain.
source: One hour following injection, dPGS-PTX-IDCC was clearly visualized within the tumor tissue but not in the normal brain (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging of brain sections shown in Figure 5B.

claim: At 24 hr following administration, dPGS-PTX-IDCC was still evident inside the tumor, though to a lesser extent.
source: At 24 hr following administration, dPGS-PTX-IDCC was still evident, though to a lesser extent, inside the tumor (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The localization of dPG-PTX-IDCC in the tumor was negligent at both 1 hr and 24 hr time points.
source: Conversely, the localization of dPG-PTX-IDCC in the tumor was negligent at both time points, with a slight increase of IDCC signal in the normal brain compared to dPGS-PTX-IDCC (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A clear co-localization between dPGS-PTX-IDCC and the tumor endothelium was shown.
source: Conversely, a clear co-localization between dPGS-PTX-IDCC and the tumor endothelium was shown (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry and confocal imaging shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Low levels of TSP-1 PM (1 ng/mL) were sufficient for complete inhibition of endothelial cells sprouting from aortic rings.
source: However, low levels of TSP-1 PM (1 ng/mL) were sufficient for complete inhibition of endothelial cells sprouting.
evidence: This is supported by aortic ring assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: TSP-1 PM inhibited VEGF-induced hyperpermeability in vivo in a miles assay following 2 days of treatment.
source: TSP-1 PM also inhibited VEGF-induced hyperpermeability in vivo in a miles assay following 2 days of treatment (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This is supported by Miles assay data shown in Figures 6C-D.

claim: Basal vessels permeability was significantly decreased in TSP-1 PM treated mice.
source: Furthermore, basal vessels permeability was found to be significantly decreased in treated mice.
evidence: This is supported by Miles assay data shown in Figures 6C-D.

claim: Tumors treated with TSP-1 PM were significantly less vascularized.
source: Tumors treated with TSP-1 PM were significantly less vascularized, expressed lower levels of VEGF, and existing blood vessels were stabilized, as shown by positive staining for α smooth muscle actin (αSMA) (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 6E-F.

claim: Tumors treated with TSP-1 PM expressed lower levels of VEGF.
source: Tumors treated with TSP-1 PM were significantly less vascularized, expressed lower levels of VEGF, and existing blood vessels were stabilized, as shown by positive staining for α smooth muscle actin (αSMA) (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 6E-F.

claim: Blood vessels in tumors treated with TSP-1 PM were stabilized, as shown by positive staining for αSMA.
source: Tumors treated with TSP-1 PM were significantly less vascularized, expressed lower levels of VEGF, and existing blood vessels were stabilized, as shown by positive staining for α smooth muscle actin (αSMA) (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 6E-F.

claim: Combination treatment of TSP-1 PM and PTX enhanced both early and late apoptosis in HUVEC compared to each treatment alone.
source: The combination treatment enhanced both early (annexin V+/PI-) and late (annexin V+/PI+) apoptosis, compared to each treatment alone (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by annexin V/PI apoptosis assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Combination of TSP-1 PM and PTX inhibited both endothelial and glioblastoma cells' sprouting to a greater extent compared to other treatment groups in 3D spheroids.
source: Combination of TSP-1 PM and PTX inhibited both endothelial and glioblastoma cells' sprouting to a greater extent compared to the other treatment groups (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by 3D spheroid invasion assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: TSP-1 PM stabilizes blood vessels in GL261 tumors.
source: αSMA staining confirmed that TSP-1 PM stabilizes blood vessels in GL261 tumors (Figure 7C), thereby enhancing the internalization of the dendritic conjugates, as demonstrated by confocal imaging of tumor sections (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: TSP-1 PM enhances the internalization of dendritic conjugates into GL261 tumors.
source: αSMA staining confirmed that TSP-1 PM stabilizes blood vessels in GL261 tumors (Figure 7C), thereby enhancing the internalization of the dendritic conjugates, as demonstrated by confocal imaging of tumor sections (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Animal survival after treatment with dPGS-PTX in combination with TSP-1 PM was significantly longer compared to the untreated control group or TMZ-treated group.
source: Animal survival after treatment with dPGS-PTX in combination with TSP-1 PM was significantly longer compared to the untreated control group or TMZ-treated group (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival curve data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Mice treated with combination of dPGS-PTX and TSP-1 PM exhibited a remarkable 100% survival rate, with all mice surviving more than 120 days.
source: Mice treated with combination of dPGS-PTX and TSP-1 PM exhibited a remarkable 100% survival rate, with all mice surviving more than 120 days.
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: 40% of mice treated with dPGS-PTX alone survived more than 120 days.
source: This was followed by 40% of mice surviving more than 120 days in the group treated with dPGS-PTX alone, 25% of mice treated with dPG-PTX and TSP-1 PM, and 10% of mice treated with dPG-PTX alone.
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: 25% of mice treated with dPG-PTX and TSP-1 PM survived more than 120 days.
source: This was followed by 40% of mice surviving more than 120 days in the group treated with dPGS-PTX alone, 25% of mice treated with dPG-PTX and TSP-1 PM, and 10% of mice treated with dPG-PTX alone.
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: 10% of mice treated with dPG-PTX alone survived more than 120 days.
source: This was followed by 40% of mice surviving more than 120 days in the group treated with dPGS-PTX alone, 25% of mice treated with dPG-PTX and TSP-1 PM, and 10% of mice treated with dPG-PTX alone.
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: TSP-1 PM as monotherapy did not result in any survival benefit.
source: Interestingly, TSP-1 PM as monotherapy did not result in any survival benefit.
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Both dPGS and dPG without PTX did not significantly affect mice survival compared to non-treated controls.
source: Both dPGS and dPG did not significantly affect mice survival compared to non-treated controls, suggesting that dPGS does not have an inhibitory effect on inflammation in a glioblastoma model to an extent that influences the therapeutic outcome.
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: No significant weight loss was observed following any of the treatments.
source: Body weight measurements showed that no significant weight loss was observed following any of the treatments (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Mice treated with dPGS-PTX plus TSP-1 PM did not exhibit any systemic toxicity.
source: Blood test results indicated that mice treated with dPGS-PTX plus TSP-1 PM did not exhibit any systemic toxicity and generally seemed healthier compared with non-treated control mice or any other treatment.
evidence: This is supported by blood test data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Myelosuppression associated with TMZ treatment was observed by decreased white blood cells count in TMZ treated mice.
source: In contrast, myelosuppression that is associated with TMZ treatment was observed by decreased white blood cells count in TMZ treated mice.
evidence: This is supported by blood count data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: High total bilirubin together with elevated liver enzymes (SGOT and SGPT) was shown in mice treated with free PTX and TMZ.
source: High total bilirubin together with elevated liver enzymes (SGOT and SGPT), an indication for liver dysfunction, was shown in mice treated with free PTX and TMZ.
evidence: This is supported by biochemistry analysis data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: Mice administered with the targeted sulfated dPGS-PTX conjugate exhibited the best performance in motor coordination tests with no motor deficit.
source: In both skills set, mice administered with the targeted sulfated dPGS-PTX conjugate exhibited the best performance with no motor deficit.
evidence: This is supported by Rotarod test data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1G-H.

claim: The non-targeted dPG-PTX conjugate caused neurotoxicity in treated mice similarly to the free drug.
source: The non-targeted dPG-PTX conjugate, though exhibited improved therapeutic outcome, caused neurotoxicity in treated mice similarly to the free drug.
evidence: This is supported by Rotarod test data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1G-H.

claim: Only combination treatment of dPGS-PTX with TSP-1 PM resulted in a marked tumor growth inhibition compared to the control group in U-87 MG tumors.
source: As shown in Figure 8C, all treatment groups were able to inhibit U-87 MG tumor growth. However, only combination treatment of dPGS-PTX with TSP-1 PM resulted in a marked tumor growth inhibition compared to the control group.
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Expression of Fas in the tumor tissue was enhanced following combination of TSP-1 PM with either dPG-PTX or dPGS-PTX.
source: Results demonstrate that expression of Fas in the tumor tissue was enhanced following combination of TSP-1 PM with either dPG-PTX or dPGS-PTX.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: A marked increase in Fas-L expression was demonstrated following treatment with combination of TSP-1 PM and dPGS-PTX.
source: Nonetheless, a marked increase in Fas-L expression was demonstrated following treatment with combination of TSP-1 PM and dPGS-PTX.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Decreased CD31 staining was demonstrated in tumors treated with dendritic conjugates.
source: Furthermore, decreased CD31 staining was demonstrated in tumors treated with our dendritic conjugates (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The resistant phenotype in glioblastoma is triggered by the activity of the O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (MGMT) DNA-repair enzyme.
source: The resistant phenotype is triggered by the activity of the O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (MGMT) DNA-repair enzyme that blunts the therapeutic effect of alkylating agents.
evidence: This is established knowledge about glioblastoma resistance mechanisms.

claim: MGMT serves as both prognostic and predictive factor in glioblastoma.
source: The identification of MGMT as the key player in the resistance to chemotherapy in glioblastoma, and the fact that it serves not only as prognostic but also as predictive factor, have made this enzyme a potential target for personalized therapy and facilitated the development of several inhibitors (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2008.

claim: Clinical trials of MGMT inhibitors have shown disappointing results with severe systemic toxicity.
source: Unfortunately, clinical trials have shown disappointing results with severe systemic toxicity (Quinn et al., 2009a; Quinn et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Quinn et al., 2009a and Quinn et al., 2009b.

claim: The potency of PTX does not depend on the cells' MGMT status.
source: The mitotic inhibitor PTX represents a potential alternative chemotherapeutic agent for glioblastoma, as its potency does not depend on the cells' MGMT status.
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanism of action of PTX compared to alkylating agents.

claim: PTX-loaded PEGylated poly(ɛ-caprolactone) nanoparticles inhibited tumor growth in mice bearing intracranial glioblastoma and prolonged their survival.
source: PTX-loaded PEGylated poly(ɛ-caprolactone) nanoparticles were demonstrated to inhibit tumor growth in mice bearing intracranial glioblastoma and prolong their survival (Xin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Xin et al., 2010.

claim: A hydrogel matrix entrapping PLGA-PTX microspheres demonstrated sustained drug release and enhanced anti-tumor efficacy when implanted into subcutaneous glioblastoma tumors.
source: A hydrogel matrix entrapping PLGA-PTX microspheres were synthesized by Ranganath and colleagues. This formulation demonstrated a sustained drug release and an enhanced anti-tumor efficacy when implanted into subcutaneous glioblastoma tumors (Ranganath et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ranganath et al., 2009.

claim: Penetration of both the BBB and the blood-tumor barrier is achieved by dPGS-PTX through extravasation-dependent 'passive' and ligand-targeted 'active' targeting.
source: We demonstrate here that penetration of both the BBB and the blood-tumor barrier is achieved by extravasation-dependent 'passive' and ligand-targeted 'active' targeting through binding of sulfate groups on the dendritic conjugate to P-/L-selectin.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo imaging and biodistribution data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Binding of the dendritic conjugate to the endothelium facilitates its extravasation via blood vessels to the target site.
source: This barrier crossing is attributed to the expression of P-selectin on activated tumor endothelial cells (Barthel et al., 2007; Läubli and Borsig, 2010; Shamay et al., 2016a), as binding of the dendritic conjugate to the endothelium facilitates its extravasation via blood vessels to the target site (Ofek et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies and data from Ofek et al., 2016.

claim: Radiation rapidly increases endothelial cell display of P-selectin on vascular lumen surfaces in a microtubule-dependent process.
source: It is also reported that radiation rapidly increases endothelial cell display of P-selectin on vascular lumen surfaces in a microtubule-dependent process (Hallahan and Virudachalam, 1999), thus sensitivity to dPGS-PTX may be further enhanced following local radiation treatment of glioma.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hallahan and Virudachalam, 1999.

claim: Sensitivity to dPGS-PTX may be further enhanced following local radiation treatment of glioma.
source: It is also reported that radiation rapidly increases endothelial cell display of P-selectin on vascular lumen surfaces in a microtubule-dependent process (Hallahan and Virudachalam, 1999), thus sensitivity to dPGS-PTX may be further enhanced following local radiation treatment of glioma.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the known effect of radiation on P-selectin expression.

claim: High expression of P-selectin correlates with poor patient survival in glioblastoma.
source: Surprisingly, a TCGA data analysis shown here has further demonstrated that high expression of P-selectin correlates with poor patient survival.
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Targeting P-selectin in glioblastoma may potentially have an additional therapeutic benefit beyond drug delivery.
source: This suggests that targeting P-selectin in glioblastoma may potentially have an additional therapeutic benefit.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the correlation between P-selectin expression and survival.

claim: ABT-510 was shown to enhance delivery of chemotherapeutics through normalization of tumor vasculature.
source: We have previously shown a correlation between loss of TSP-1 expression and escape from dormancy in human glioblastoma (Satchi-Fainaro et al., 2012). Thus, glioma stimulation of local endothelium should be mitigated by restoration of TSP-1 function. TSP-1 PM used here is a second generation peptide of ABT-510, which was shown to enhance the efficacy of both PTX and of cisplatin in an orthotopic syngeneic model of ovarian cancer through normalization of tumor vasculature, as documented by increased pericytes coating tumor vessels, leading to increased concentration of these agents in the tumor (Campbell et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Campbell et al., 2010.

claim: A similar mechanism of synergy through vascular normalization was reported when administering bevacizumab prior to PTX.
source: A similar mechanism of synergy was also reported when administering the anti-angiogenic agent bevacizumab prior to PTX (Tolaney et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tolaney et al., 2015.

claim: Enhanced tumor growth inhibition and long-term survival may be mainly due to vascular normalization by TSP-1 PM.
source: Thus, enhanced tumor growth inhibition and long-term survival may be mainly due to vascular normalization.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed effects and literature precedent.

claim: dPGS-PTX may synergize with TSP-1 PM by inducing the Fas/Fas-L apoptosis pathway.
source: Alternatively, increased in vitro endothelial cell presentation of Fas (CD95) was observed with >1 nM concentrations of docetaxel, and ABT-510-dependent apoptosis of tumor endothelial cells was shown to be induced by their upregulation of Fas ligand (CD178) (Yap et al., 2005). We postulated that dPGS-PTX may similarly synergize TSP-1 PM by inducing the Fas/Fas-L apoptosis pathway.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on literature precedent and supported by IHC data in the manuscript.

claim: IHC analysis supported the hypothesis that dPGS-PTX synergizes with TSP-1 PM through the Fas/Fas-L apoptosis pathway.
source: IHC analysis supported this hypothesis, suggesting an additional mechanism which contributes to the enhanced anti-tumor effect observed in our in vivo studies.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Both vascular normalization and Fas/Fas-L pathway induction mechanisms may operate and be mutually amplifying.
source: Both of the putative mechanisms may operate and be mutually amplifying.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential interaction of two mechanisms.

claim: The combination of TSP-1 PM and dPGS-PTX has tremendous potential in replacing conventional therapy for glioblastoma patients with high MGMT activity.
source: In conclusion, the work described here demonstrates the tremendous potential of our novel combination of TSP-1 PM and dPGS-PTX in replacing the conventional therapy for those patients who will not benefit from alkylating agents (i.e., high MGMT activity), with decreased toxicity and increased safety profile.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in the manuscript.
